extracted.intended_audience: public speakers, humorists, and general readers of Mark Twain
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples drawn from Mark Twain's delivered speeches on how to compose and present humorous oratory, including conduct, language, persona, and topical scope. The page is a collection of exemplar speeches rather than a formal how-to, but it contains many prescriptive remarks about speaking and writing for public audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, tell the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A maxim Twain claims as his own: “When in doubt, tell the truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain presents this as a practical emergency principle he uses and offers it as a legacy to listeners—short, pithy moral guidance for conduct and for resolving difficult moments in speech or life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewers should not reproduce speech in the first person
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'altogether wrong' to interview a man and reproduce his spoken words in the first person; an interviewer should give the substance and put it in his own language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain explains that a first-person reproduction inevitably misrepresents the speaker—either 'better language' or 'worse'—and in his case is usually worse. Practical implication: public figures and speakers should be cautious about relying on press interviews and interviewers should paraphrase rather than fake first-person quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the best English; avoid slang and degradation of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain asserts a 'great respect for the English language' and says he strives to 'use the best English' and 'never to degrade it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He criticizes interviewers who invent slang in his mouth and says he would rather remain silent than use language he deems unworthy. For speakers/writers: prefer precise, elevated language over gratuitous slang or sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too much truth can damage literature
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I don't know anything that mars good literature so completely as too much truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain advises that while facts contain poetry, an excess of literal truth can harm literary quality. Implication for humorists and writers: select and shape facts—balance truth and invention for literary/humorous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: On formal/complimentary occasions, confine remarks to compliments
rubrics_metrics.description: 'On an occasion like this the proprieties require that you merely pay compliments to the guest of the occasion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain emphasizes etiquette for toasts and ceremonial replies: such settings call for complimentary, noncritical remarks. Speakers should avoid public criticism and stick to the expected decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain or assume a character/persona
rubrics_metrics.description: 'One must keep up one's character. Earn a character first if you can, and if you can't, then assume one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain recommends cultivating a consistent public persona; if a speaker lacks an earned reputation, they should consciously adopt a character to present. This is guidance for performance consistency and audience expectation management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include at least one serious point amid levity
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain worries that his talk has been 'so much levity' that he has 'said no serious thing' and resolves to leave the audience with 'one serious word' they can carry home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For effective humorous speeches, mix levity with at least one substantial, memorable serious insight so the audience gains value beyond entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress and appearance are part of public presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain discusses clothing (preference for white clothes, desire to be conspicuous) as part of how one presents oneself in assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He treats dress humorously but prescriptively: appearance can create distinction, affect reception, and be used deliberately as part of a stage persona. Speakers should consider costume/attire as a rhetorical tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: When commemorating civic events, address multiple dimensions (sentimental, commercial, historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain criticizes speeches that treat a celebration from only its 'sentimental, patriotic, poetic side' and insists the day 'has a commercial, a business side that needs reforming. It has a historical side.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For addresses on public anniversaries or civic topics, examine and acknowledge different aspects (emotional, economic, historical) rather than a single angle; this produces a more rounded, persuasive speech.
